title: Plan and direct extensive livestock farming activities

lessons.title: Planning the extensive farming year
lessons.html:
Planning the extensive farming year

In this work experience module you plan and direct the livestock activities of an extensive farm, or a section of it, under the guidance of the farm manager. You will produce plans, direct teams and report on results.

Start with the resources

Before planning, understand what the farm has:

  • Land and veld: camps, sizes, veld type and condition, carrying capacity guidelines for the area.
  • Water: boreholes, pumps, reservoirs and their capacity.
  • Animals: numbers and classes from the stock register.
  • Infrastructure: kraals, crushes, dip tank, loading ramp, fences, roads.
  • People and equipment: team skills, vehicles, tools.
  • Budget: approved spending on feed, lick, health and repairs.

The annual plan

Build a calendar with the manager that sets the breeding season, expected birth season, weaning, sales, shearing (if applicable), vaccinations, parasite control, lick changes, veld burning or fire-break preparation, and maintenance periods. Check that the plan is realistic for labour and money in each month.

Grazing plan

Allocate camps to herds or flocks over the year so that each camp gets its planned rest. Match the number of animals to the forage available. Plan a drought reserve - camps or fodder kept back - and decide in advance at what point animals will be sold if rain fails.

Budget and inputs

Estimate quantities and costs of lick, feed, remedies and fuel per month. Plan orders ahead of need, especially for products with long delivery times or seasonal price increases.

Present the plan

Present your plan to the manager, explain assumptions, accept feedback and finalise it. Share the relevant parts with team leaders in simple, practical terms.

lessons.title: Directing activities across the farm
lessons.html:
Directing activities across the farm

Weekly cycle

Run a steady weekly cycle: plan on Monday, brief team leaders, monitor during the week, and review on Friday. Adjust plans when weather, animal health or breakdowns require it.

Directing teams

  • Give team leaders clear objectives, deadlines and resources.
  • Allocate skilled people to critical tasks such as vaccination, pump repairs and handling bulls.
  • Visit the work: kraal days, camp moves, water rounds.
  • Check quality against standards, give feedback and coach.
  • Make sure safety rules and PPE are followed under the OHS Act 85 of 1993.

Coordinating with others

Extensive farming involves people outside the team: the vet, feed suppliers, auctioneers, transporters, neighbours (for shared fences and fire breaks), the local fire protection association and sometimes the state vet. Schedule their involvement in time and keep them informed.

Handling the unexpected

EventFirst actions
Borehole pump fails in summerMove animals to another water source or cart water; call the technician
Veld fireRaise the alarm, move animals and people to safety, call the fire protection association; never put people in danger
Suspected disease outbreakStop movements, isolate, call vet and state vet
Stock theftCount, check fences and tracks, report to the police stock theft unit at once

Compliance

Ensure animal welfare, disease control, identification, withdrawal periods, water use and soil conservation duties are met. Relevant laws include the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962, Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984, Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 and National Water Act 36 of 1998.

lessons.title: Reviewing results and reporting
lessons.html:
Reviewing results and reporting

Monitoring indicators

Track a short list of indicators each month and at the end of each season:

  • Stock numbers by class and reconciliation with the register.
  • Conception and weaning percentages.
  • Mortality by age group and cause.
  • Weaning weights and sale weights.
  • Body condition of breeding females at key times.
  • Veld condition and rainfall.
  • Costs per animal against budget.

Analysing results

Compare results with targets and with previous years. Look for causes: a lower weaning percentage might come from poor condition at breeding, a bull problem, disease or predators. Use records, field observations, and input from the vet and team to find the most likely cause.

Writing the report

Your work experience report to the manager should include:

  1. A short summary of the period.
  2. What was planned and what was done.
  3. Key indicators against targets, in a table.
  4. Problems encountered and actions taken.
  5. Financial summary against budget.
  6. Recommendations for the next season.

Keep it factual and clear. Attach supporting records where useful.

Improving the plan

Use what you learned to improve next year's plan: adjust stocking rates, change the timing of the breeding season, revise the lick programme or improve predator control. Involve the team in the review; they often have practical solutions.

Your portfolio

Keep copies of your plans, schedules, briefing notes, reports and the manager's feedback as evidence for assessment.

Key points

  • Plan from the farm's real resources: veld, water, animals, people and budget.
  • Keep a drought reserve and decide trigger points in advance.
  • Direct through a weekly plan, brief and review cycle.
  • Have first actions ready for pump failure, fire, disease and theft.
  • Report indicators against targets and use the review to improve the plan.
